books.title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
books.author: Dale Carnegie
books.description: The classic on getting along with people, with advice that still works nearly a century later.
ideas: Don't criticize, condemn or complain

When someone is criticised, they rarely think, "You're right, I'll change." They get defensive, justify themselves and often resent the critic. Dale Carnegie observed that even people who have done terrible things usually believe they had good reasons. Criticism wounds pride and seldom changes behaviour. Understanding works better: try to see why the person acted as they did. Today: the next time you're tempted to criticise someone, pause and ask yourself what might have led them there, and respond with curiosity first.
Become genuinely interested in others

Carnegie's famous line is that you'll make more friends in two months by becoming interested in other people than in two years of trying to get them interested in you. People light up when someone genuinely wants to know about their lives, work and passions. It's not a technique; it has to be real curiosity. And almost everyone has something fascinating to share if you ask. Today: in your next conversation, ask two follow-up questions about something the other person cares about, and really listen to the answers.
Remember names

A person's name is, to them, one of the most important sounds in any language. Using it shows that you see them as an individual, not just another face. Carnegie tells of leaders who made a point of remembering names, and how much loyalty that earned. Forgetting someone's name, on the other hand, can feel like a small dismissal. Today: when you meet someone new, repeat their name in conversation and write it down later if needed. Use it the next time you see them.
Talk in terms of their interests

If you want to persuade someone, Carnegie advises, start from what they care about, not what you want. A child doesn't care that you want them to eat vegetables; they might care about being strong enough to win at football. A colleague might not care about your deadline, but they care about a smooth week for their team. Speaking to people's interests isn't manipulation when it's honest; it's respect. Today: before asking someone for something, think about how it could genuinely benefit them, and lead with that.
Let the other person save face

Even when you're completely right, embarrassing someone in front of others rarely helps. Carnegie notes that people remember being humiliated long after they've forgotten the issue. Letting someone save face, by correcting them privately, giving them an easy way to change their mind and acknowledging what they did well, keeps the relationship intact. Today: if you need to point out someone's mistake, do it privately and kindly, and give them room to fix it without losing dignity.

books.title: Crucial Conversations
books.author: Patterson, Grenny, McMillan & Switzler
books.description: Tools for talking when stakes are high, opinions differ and emotions run strong.
ideas: Start with heart

Before a high-stakes talk, it's easy to slip into wanting to win: proving you're right, getting the last word. The authors of Crucial Conversations suggest starting with heart. Ask yourself what you really want for yourself, for the other person and for the relationship. That question shifts your focus from scoring points to solving the problem together. Today: before a difficult conversation, write down your honest answers to those three questions.
Make it safe

When people feel unsafe in a conversation, they tend to go silent or turn aggressive. Neither leads to good solutions. The authors recommend watching for signs that safety is breaking down, like sarcasm, withdrawal or raised voices, and then restoring it by showing respect and clarifying the shared goal. People can hear almost anything when they feel safe. Today: if a conversation turns tense, pause and say something like, "I want us both to get what we need here."
Separate facts from stories

"You were late three times this week" is a fact. "You don't care about the team" is a story we've built on top of it. The authors suggest separating the two: lead with the facts and offer your interpretation tentatively, as a possibility rather than a verdict. This invites the other person to explain instead of defend. Today: in your next disagreement, start with what you observed, then say, "The story I'm telling myself is…", and ask how they see it.
Fill the pool of shared meaning

Good decisions come from having everyone's views on the table, especially the uncomfortable ones. The authors call this filling the pool of shared meaning. When people hold back, decisions are worse and commitment is weaker. Inviting disagreement, and listening without punishing it, makes the pool richer. Today: in your next group discussion, ask specifically for opposing views, and thank people who offer them.

books.title: Nonviolent Communication
books.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
books.description: A four-part method for expressing yourself honestly and listening with empathy.
ideas: Observe without judging

Marshall Rosenberg noticed that much conflict begins with a judgment disguised as an observation. "You're so lazy" invites a fight; "You left the dishes in the sink last night" invites a conversation. His method starts by describing what happened as a camera would, without labels or exaggerations. It's harder than it sounds, because judgments come naturally. Today: in your next complaint, try to state only what you actually saw or heard, with no interpretation.
Express feelings

After observing, Rosenberg suggests expressing your feelings with real feeling words: worried, frustrated, relieved, lonely. He notes that "I feel that you're ignoring me" isn't actually a feeling; it's a thought about the other person. Naming genuine feelings makes you more understandable and less threatening. Today: when you share a frustration, finish the sentence "I feel…" with an emotion rather than an accusation.
Connect feelings to needs

Behind every feeling, Rosenberg believed, is a need: for rest, respect, connection, safety or understanding. Linking your feelings to your needs helps others see what's really going on and makes it easier for them to help. "I feel anxious because I need some predictability" opens a door that "You're so unreliable" slams shut. Today: when you feel upset, ask yourself which need isn't being met, and mention it when you talk about it.
Make clear requests

The final step in Rosenberg's method is a clear, specific, doable request, not a vague demand. "Could you text me if you'll be late tonight?" is far easier to say yes to than "Be more considerate." A real request also leaves room for a no; otherwise it's a demand in disguise. Today: turn one complaint into a specific request that the other person could easily act on.

books.title: Never Split the Difference
books.author: Chris Voss
books.description: A former FBI hostage negotiator's techniques for everyday negotiations.
ideas: Tactical empathy

Chris Voss, a former FBI hostage negotiator, says the most powerful tool in any negotiation is tactical empathy: showing the other side that you understand their position and feelings, even if you don't agree. People open up when they feel heard. It works with kidnappers, landlords and teenagers alike. Today: in your next disagreement, summarise the other person's view so well that they say, "Exactly." Only then share your own.
Mirroring

One of Voss's simplest techniques is mirroring: repeating the last few words someone said, with a curious tone, as a question. "We need it by Friday." "By Friday?" It sounds almost too simple, but it encourages people to keep talking and reveal more about what they need. Today: try mirroring once in a conversation and notice how the other person expands on their point.
Label emotions

Naming emotions out loud, "It seems like you're frustrated about the timeline", can defuse them. Voss calls this labelling. It shows understanding without agreeing, and it often lowers the temperature of a tense conversation. Interestingly, labelling negative emotions tends to weaken them, while labelling positive ones reinforces them. Today: in a tense moment, try a label that starts with "It seems like…" or "It sounds like…" and pause afterwards.
Aim for "that's right"

Voss believes the words "that's right" are more valuable than "yes" in a negotiation. People often say yes just to end the conversation, but "that's right" means they genuinely feel understood. Reaching that point usually means summarising their view accurately, including their feelings. Real agreement becomes possible from there. Today: aim to get a "that's right" in your next difficult conversation by summarising the other person's perspective.
Calibrated questions

Questions starting with "how" or "what" invite the other side to think about your problem. Voss calls them calibrated questions: "How am I supposed to do that?", "What's most important to you here?" They're softer than demands and harder to refuse, and they give the other person a sense of control while steering the conversation. Today: replace one demand in a negotiation with a "how" or "what" question, and see how the other person responds.

books.title: Talk Like TED
books.author: Carmine Gallo
books.description: Lessons from the most popular TED talks on giving presentations people remember.
ideas: Unleash your passion

The most memorable talks, Carmine Gallo found, come from speakers who clearly love their subject. Passion is contagious: audiences connect with enthusiasm more than with polish. If you're bored by your topic, your listeners will be too. Before giving a talk, find the part of the subject that genuinely excites you. Today: when you next have to present something, ask yourself what fascinates you about it and start there.
Tell stories

Stories stick in memory far better than data alone. Gallo noticed that popular talks often wrap their key points in personal, vivid stories: a moment of failure, a surprising encounter, a turning point. Data persuades the mind; stories move the heart. Today: take one point you want to make at work or home and find a short story that illustrates it.
Keep it to 18 minutes

TED talks are limited to about eighteen minutes, and Gallo argues that's no accident. Long talks overload the brain; shorter ones force speakers to cut ruthlessly and focus on what really matters. Constraints sharpen messages. Today: take your next presentation and challenge yourself to deliver it in half the time. Notice what you choose to keep.
Deliver jaw-dropping moments

Audiences remember one striking moment more than a dozen good points: a surprising demonstration, a shocking statistic, an unexpected object or a powerful image. Gallo calls these jaw-dropping moments, and they're what people talk about afterwards. Today: think of one surprising fact, image or demonstration that could make your next presentation memorable.
